strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in visual design: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing in posters and complex layouts without requiring explicit font labels or test-time optimization.

The data curation and content-style decoupling pipeline is well thought out, leveraging a fine-tuned VLM-based OCR (Qwen2.5-VL) and DINOv2 style verification to produce 100k clean, paired training examples.

The conditioning strategy is simple and parameter-efficient: utilizing a frozen VAE encoder to project both the reference context and glyph map directly into the DiT latent sequence, avoiding complex auxiliary modules like ControlNets.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate strong results across several benchmarks, including poster text editing, standard scene text benchmarks (AnyText), and even zero-shot generalization to handwritten text synthesis (IAM and CVL).
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the core architecture is somewhat incremental; concatenating VAE latents of condition images along the sequence dimension in DiT backbones and applying spatially weighted loss masks are fairly standard techniques in recent diffusion and flow-matching literature.

Details regarding the data synthesis pipeline in Section 3.2 are slightly ambiguous: the authors mention using existing 'editing models to replace the original content while preserving all typographical attributes' to create the 100k training pairs, which leaves it unclear which models were used and how reliable they were prior to filtering.

The in-house benchmark consists of only 200 samples, and the paper lacks a structured human evaluation or user study, which is particularly relevant for assessing aesthetic fidelity and typographic adherence in graphic design workflows.

Although Section 3.5 introduces DMD2 distillation for 8-step fast inference, the experimental section does not include quantitative evaluations or ablation comparisons between the distilled student model and the teacher model in terms of speed versus quality trade-offs.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical challenge in design workflows: performing text editing while maintaining fine-grained control over font typography and stylistic nuances from visual exemplars without requiring font category labels or test-time fine-tuning.

Presents a well-conceived data curation and content-style decoupling pipeline, using a fine-tuned vision-language model (Qwen2.5-VL) to transcribe ornate/calligraphic scripts and enforcing content decoupling with LLM text generation followed by dual verification (OCR + DINOv2).

The conditioning strategy is simple and effective: leveraging frozen VAE encoding of reference posters and glyph patches concatenated directly along the sequence dimension, avoiding heavy auxiliary networks or specialized ControlNet branches.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse settings: outperforms prior baselines on poster editing, scene text editing (AnyText benchmark in English and Chinese), and demonstrates surprising zero-shot transfer to handwritten line generation (IAM and CVL benchmarks).
weaknesses: The architectural design is somewhat incremental: concatenating VAE latents of visual context images along the sequence dimension of a DiT backbone is a standard pattern established by recent models like FLUX Kontext and Qwen-Image-Edit. The technical novelty lies predominantly in the data generation and conditioning setup rather than architectural innovation.

Ambiguity in the synthetic data creation pipeline: Section 3.2 mentions using 'editing models to replace the original content while preserving all typographical attributes' to produce the 100k training pairs. Given that the paper argues existing editing models fail at precise font preservation, it is unclear which editing model was used to create this initial training corpus and how severe the data filtering attrition rate was.

Incomplete evaluation of the inference acceleration claim: While Section 3.5 describes distilling the model with DMD2 into an 8-step student to achieve a 10x speedup, no quantitative or qualitative comparison between the teacher and the 8-step distilled student is provided in the experiments.
The in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark contains only 200 samples, which is relatively small for drawing broad statistical conclusions on diverse typographic styles.
Minor presentation flaws and typos throughout the text (e.g., 'handwrittent' in the Abstract, 'specificly' on page 7, and 'the analyze on the weight' on page 8).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical application in graphic design and visual text editing: enabling fine-grained, font-controllable text replacement without requiring font category labels or per-instance test-time fine-tuning.

The empirical evaluation is broad, testing across poster benchmarks, standard scene text benchmarks (AnyText), and handwritten text generation (IAM and CVL), demonstrating competitive quantitative results across multiple metrics (Sen. Acc, NED, DINO similarity, HWD).

The dual-stream visual conditioning avoids adding heavy external encoders by directly encoding reference images via the frozen VAE into the sequence dimension, keeping the architecture straightforward.
weaknesses: Limited architectural and conceptual novelty: The core framework relies almost entirely on existing tools and conventional techniques—fine-tuning Qwen-Image-Edit with LoRA, standard VAE latent sequence concatenation, spatially weighted diffusion loss, and standard DMD2 distillation.

Ambiguity and potential circularity in data curation: In Section 3.2, the authors state that they 'leverage editing models to replace the original content while preserving all typographical attributes' to construct the 100k training pairs. It is unclear which editing models are used and how they reliably preserved fine-grained typography if existing models struggle with this exact task. The lack of detailed specifications for this critical pipeline severely hampers reproducibility.

Unclear handling of character sets and arbitrary glyph references: The method relies on a reference glyph map $X_g$ rendered onto a canvas matching the input poster size. It remains ambiguous how user-provided glyph patches are mapped when the target text contains characters not present in the reference patch (out-of-vocabulary character generalization), or how layout alignment is established during inference.

Trade-off between font conditioning and text accuracy: In Table 4, introducing Font Style Reference (FSR) causes a substantial drop in Sentence Accuracy (from 93.27% down to 83.34%) and NED (from 0.9734 to 0.9502). While the authors attribute this partly to OCR evaluation difficulties, it indicates that conditioning on complex font references significantly degrades character legibility and recognition fidelity.
The SkyReels-Text benchmark consists of only 200 samples, which is relatively small for drawing definitive statistical conclusions regarding complex multi-font text editing.

strengths: Practical and timely formulation: Addressing arbitrary font control and style-consistent text replacement in complex poster/artistic layouts without requiring explicit font labels or test-time optimization fills an important gap in modern image editing workflows.

Well-engineered data decoupling pipeline: The synthesis workflow utilizing Qwen3-8B for divergent text generation, Nano Banana for initial editing, SAM2 for segmentation, and a dual-verification mechanism (VLM-OCR content check + DINOv2 style check) is thoughtful, scalable, and effectively decouples text content from font style across 100K training pairs.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative validation: Demonstrates solid improvements over strong baselines (FLUX-Text, AnyText, Calligrapher, Qwen-Image-Edit) across scene text benchmarks (AnyText benchmark, SkyReels-Text benchmark), handwriting synthesis benchmarks (IAM, CVL), as well as multi-font poster editing scenarios.
Practical inference distillation: Adapting DMD2 into an 8-step student model achieves a >10x speedup while retaining typographic control and visual quality, enhancing real-world usability.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on proprietary/external tools in dataset creation: The 100K training pair generation relies on a closed/commercial tool (Nano Banana) alongside Qwen models; the exact prompts, failure filtering rates, and reproducibility of this data generation step should be detailed more transparently.

Evaluation metric circularity/bias: The primary text fidelity metrics (Sen. Acc. and NED) on the SkyReels-Text benchmark are evaluated using the authors' own fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL 7B model (Section 4.3), which introduces potential evaluation bias compared to using independent, standard third-party OCR engines.

Limited architectural novelty: The core model architecture mostly concatenates frozen VAE latents of the plain-text template and glyph map with the noisy latent before feeding into an off-the-shelf DiT backbone (Qwen-Image-Edit) with LoRA. The contribution lies predominantly in the data generation pipeline and task formulation rather than algorithmic/architectural breakthroughs.

strengths: Practical and timely problem: Fine-grained, font-controllable text editing in poster design without requiring font labels, pre-installed font files, or test-time optimization addresses a well-recognized bottleneck in AI-assisted graphic design workflows.

Effective data engine and content-style decoupling pipeline: Curating real poster data and decoupling font style from textual content using LLM substitution, localized editing, and dual-verification (OCR match and DINO feature similarity) is a pragmatic and well-designed strategy to obtain high-quality paired supervision (100K pairs).

Extensive experimental evaluation: The paper evaluates across diverse domains, including poster editing benchmarks, standard scene text editing (AnyText English/Chinese benchmarks), and zero-shot handwritten text synthesis (IAM and CVL datasets), achieving superior or highly competitive quantitative and qualitative performance across all settings.

Thorough ablation and practical engineering: The ablations on visual font referencing and text-region loss reweighting validate key design decisions, and applying DMD2 distillation to achieve an 8-step inference pipeline makes the system practical for real-world interactive design.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation bias with customized metrics: For the in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark (Table 1), text recognition metrics (Sen. Acc. and NED) are computed using the authors' own fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL 7B model rather than standard third-party OCR engines, and style adherence is evaluated with DINO (the same objective used during dataset filtering). This self-referential evaluation loop raises questions about fairness when comparing against baseline models.

Architectural novelty is largely compositional: The underlying architecture relies heavily on fine-tuning an existing foundation model (Qwen-Image-Edit via LoRA) with channel/sequence concatenation of VAE-encoded visual references and a masked loss weighting. While effective, the technical contribution lies more in system integration and data curation rather than fundamental architectural breakthroughs.

Unclear implementation details for multi-font spatial mapping: The paper demonstrates impressive multi-font editing in Figure 15, but Section 3.3 is vague regarding how multiple heterogeneous glyph patches $g_i$ are mapped onto the input canvas $X_{glyph}$ and paired unambiguously with their corresponding regional masks $r_i$ without cross-talk.

Heavy reliance on external proprietary pipelines for data creation: The dataset generation depends on models like Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) and large proprietary models for inpainting and text replacement. Potential synthetic artifacts or constraints from these upstream models and issues of open reproducibility warrant deeper discussion.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical design task: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing in complex graphic layouts (such as posters) guided directly by visual glyph patches, without requiring font labels or test-time optimization.

A well-engineered data synthesis and curation pipeline: the authors design a content-style decoupling framework integrating LLM substitution, local editing, SAM2 segmentation, and a rigorous dual-verification gate (VLM-based OCR and DINOv2 similarity), yielding 100K high-quality paired training samples.

Effective architectural and training design: dual-stream visual conditioning via frozen VAE latent concatenation alongside text-region weighted loss and DMD2 distillation provides strong control and efficient 8-step inference.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: the method is evaluated across poster editing, standard scene text benchmarks (AnyText), and cross-domain zero-shot handwritten text generation (IAM and CVL), demonstrating clear improvements over both open-source and leading commercial editing baselines.

High visual quality and flexibility: qualitative results show compelling rendering of intricate typographic styles (3D metallic textures, chromatic brushwork, multi-region/multi-font simultaneous editing).
weaknesses: Technical novelty of the core model architecture is somewhat modest: the framework largely fine-tunes Qwen-Image-Edit with LoRA and concatenates VAE latents of visual conditions along the sequence dimension, meaning much of the performance gain stems from data curation and engineering rather than foundational model innovations.

Heavy reliance on proprietary models in the data curation pipeline: the content-style decoupling pipeline depends on commercial black-box models (e.g., Nano Banana / Gemini 2.5 Flash Image), which introduces reproducibility hurdles for independent researchers attempting to regenerate or scale the dataset.

Potential evaluation bias: text accuracy on the SkyReels-Text benchmark is measured using the authors' own fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL 7B model, and style consistency is measured via DINOv2 (which is also used as a thresholding filter during dataset curation), potentially introducing evaluation circularity.

Insufficient discussion of failure cases and boundary conditions: the paper provides limited analysis regarding edge cases such as extreme length discrepancies between reference glyphs and target text, curved/warped non-planar typography, or missing character glyphs.
